text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Economists warned yesterday it was too early to say the economy had turned the corner in relation to the labour market, regardless of the unexpected fall in the jobless rate reported by the Australian Bureau of Statistics yesterday, with the unemployment ate at 8.5 per cent, down from October's 8.8 per cent. Page 1.

Australians in Melbourne will now be able to receive free-to-air TV live from Europe with a new VCR-sized DigiScan satellite receiver from Melbourne's Skandia Electronics Pty Ltd. The move represents the loosening of control over Australian's viewing by new Federal Government policy. Page 2.

According to Australia's biggest employer association, the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the Australian economy is in a slump with real economic growth at levels well below the national account estimates. The association also said yesterday that if the Australian Industrial Relations Commission granted the ACTU claim for its living wage case the Reserve Bank would certainly lift interest rates. Page 3.

The Productivity Commission claims the present framework of Commonwealth purchasing policy is at odds with international trends and will limit opportunities for Australian companies to access the A$800 billion international Government procurement market, warning key elements of Commonwealth policy were likely to breach the World Trade Organisation Agreement on Government Procurement. Page 4.
THE AUSTRALIAN

In a move that will rival the upcoming Telstra float, one of Australia's largest financial institutions, the AMP Society, is to embark on a major stock market float - estimated to be worth up to A$10 billion. AMP's 2.3 million policy holders are to be offered the chance to swap their membership rights for shares in the group. Approximately 40 per cent of Australian households that own an AMP product will be eligible for the shares. Page 1. --

A day after the Reserve Bank cut official interest rates, the latest unemployment figures have brought an early Christmas gift to the Federal Government. Strong growth cut the national unemployment rate from 8.8 per cent to 8.5 per cent during November. However the creation of 24,400 new jobs during November did not offset the fourth consecutive increase in youth unemployment which now sits at 29.7 per cent. Page 1.

A terminally ill woman has made a public appeal for a Northern Territory cancer specialist to support her bid to die under the controversial voluntary euthanasia law. Janet Mills, 52, who suffers from a rare form of skin cancer, engaged the services of doctor Philip Nitschke, the NT doctor who helped the first person to die under the law. Page 1.

Under a Federal Government deal with the Democrats and in a move which offers an olive branch to doctors who have staged massive demonstrations in recent weeks, junior doctors will have access to an extra 250 one-off training positions in general practice for the next three years on the condition they practice in a rural area for a decade. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The AMP Society has announced plans to offer its 2.3 million policy holders a chance to take up shares in a A$10 billion float which is tipped to rival the Federal Government's Telstra partial-sale. If the proposal is adopted by AMP members, an estimated one-in-four Australian households will receive shares in the group which last year posted a profit of A$1.9 billion. Page 1.

Australia is to join a historic trade agreement to abolish world-wide tariffs in the information technology industry. The agreement, hailed as a huge advance for the world economy, was thrashed out over three-days of intense negotiation at the World Trade Organisation meeting in Singapore. With players including the US, the European Union and Japan coming to the party, the plan is tipped to come into fruition by next July. Page 1.

Unemployment figures took a surprising dive for November, falling down to 8.5 per cent from 8.8 per cent. The Australian Bureau of Statistics figures revealed the unemployment rate in New South Wales was at 7.5 per cent -the lowest for the nation. Tasmania had the highest rate at 10.1 per cent while other States hover above the nine per cent mark. Prime Minister Howard welcomed the figures, claiming they were right on track with Budget forecasts of 8.25 per cent by June next year. Page 2.

According to a new NSW Government report, Turning Victims into Criminals, children in State care, through no fault of their own, are at least 15 times more likely to end up in a juvenile jail than other children. Although State wards live in Government institutions due to family problems or parental death, the report also reveals that female wards are 35 times more likely to enter a juvenile detention centre than other girls. Page 3.
THE AGE

Janet Mills yesterday gave a press conference in which she told reporters she had come to Darwin to make use of the voluntary euthanasia laws that she had found almost impossible to use. Mills already has two of the needed signatures, one from physician Philip Nitschke and one from psychiatrist Chris Lloyd, all she requires is one from a Northern Territory specialist. Page A2.

Senior Constable Dale William Salisbury yesterday admitted he was one of three police officers who were in a police car on 30 September 1994 that did not stop after hitting another car. Other officers involved have testified that they lied in statements relating to the hit-and-run incident and are being charged with attempting to pervert the course of justice. Page A2.

Prime Minister John Howard yesterday defended his Government's cuts to Legal Aid, saying the funding cuts would not lead to greater violence against women, stating "any example or incidence of violence against women in the Australian community was absolutely unacceptable...and utterly repugnant". Page A3.

The Retail Confectionery and Mixed Business Association said yesterday that most of its 3500 milk bar, convenience store, take-away food and sandwich bar members in Victoria had agreed to comply with a new code of conduct that was aimed at reducing the amount of under-age smoking. The new policy requires stores to ask for identification if they are uncertain if the customer is not over 18. Page A3.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
